strengths: The paper targets an important and realistic forecasting setting: multivariate series with channel-wise sampling rates, cross-channel dependencies, and block-wise missing intervals at test time.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer is a coherent architecture: channel tokens provide a natural way to summarize variable-length per-channel patches, and the masked attention design is well aligned with the stated problem.

The empirical section is fairly broad, covering modified public benchmarks, one industrial LNG dataset, multiple model families, ablations, masking-strategy variants, and conventional forecasting benchmarks.
The ablation results support the usefulness of the main components, especially patch masking under block-wise missingness and dynamic patching under asynchronous sampling.
The paper is generally clear and includes detailed appendices on dataset construction, hyperparameters, full results, and additional analyses.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol gives the proposed model a structural advantage: baselines are forced into interpolation or zero-filling pipelines, while CTF is explicitly designed and trained with masking. Stronger missing-aware or irregular-time baselines, imputation-plus-forecasting baselines, and similarly augmented baselines are needed.

The practical benchmark construction is partly synthetic and hand-designed. Sampling periods for public datasets are assigned based on plausibility rather than being naturally observed, so the real-world validity of the setting is not fully established.

The gains are often modest, especially in Scenario 1 and conventional forecasting, and some comparisons show baselines close to or better than CTF on particular datasets/settings. This weakens the claim of broad superiority.

The missingness evaluation is concentrated mainly on SolarWind, with ETT1 appearing only in the appendix; broader missingness experiments across all datasets would better support the robustness claims.

The method details leave some ambiguities, including how dominant FFT frequencies are selected robustly, whether patch lengths are fixed per channel or vary per instance, and how edge cases with weak/noisy spectra are handled.
Reproducibility is limited by the use of a private industrial CHS dataset and by insufficient detail about baseline tuning under the modified asynchronous setting.
The spectral-distortion argument is plausible but somewhat overemphasized relative to the empirical evidence; the reported frequency-domain differences between CTF and TimeXer are small.
Scalability is a real concern because the unified attention grows with all local and channel tokens, and the paper only acknowledges this limitation rather than evaluating runtime/memory tradeoffs.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: multivariate forecasting with channel-wise sampling heterogeneity and block-wise missing inputs, which is a real limitation of many standard forecasting benchmarks.

The proposed architecture is coherent: channel tokens provide a plausible way to summarize variable-length per-channel observations, and the masking scheme gives a clean mechanism for excluding fully missing patches.

The evaluation includes several modern forecasting baselines, ablations over channel dependence/dynamic patching/patch masking, error bars over seeds, and one real-world industrial dataset in addition to modified public benchmarks.
weaknesses: The main experimental setting is largely synthetic and author-constructed. The public benchmarks are manually resampled according to assumed domain-specific rates, but the paper does not convincingly justify that these modifications preserve realistic data-generating structure or yield a broadly meaningful benchmark.

The baseline comparison is not sufficiently fair or complete for the central claims. Most baselines are forced into interpolation or zero-filling, while the proposed method receives explicit masks and is trained with random patch masking. Missing-data and irregular-sampling methods discussed in related work, such as BRITS, GRU-D, RAINDROP, SERT, continuous-time/irregular time-series models, or imputation-plus-forecasting pipelines, are not evaluated.

The reported gains are often modest in Scenario 1, sometimes only a few percent over strong baselines such as PatchTST or CrossGNN. Given the customized evaluation protocol, these margins do not provide strong evidence of a robust general contribution.

The novelty is limited. Channel/global tokens, masked attention, patch dropout/random masking, channel embeddings, and frequency-aware patching are all close to existing ideas; the paper presents a useful combination but not a clearly novel algorithmic advance at top-tier level.

Important methodological details are underspecified, including how a 'strong dominant frequency' is detected, how patch lengths are bounded, how partial missing patches are handled, and how hyperparameters are selected for baselines versus the proposed model.

The block-missing evaluation is narrow: the main Scenario 2 table is only on SolarWind, with ETT1 results relegated to the appendix and no broad evaluation across all datasets. The missingness process is also tailored to the proposed patch-level masking mechanism, especially when missing blocks span exactly one patch.

The real-world CHS dataset is private or insufficiently described for reproducibility, and only 10 of 52 channels are selected without a strong selection protocol. This weakens the real-world evidence.

The paper acknowledges scalability issues but does not quantify runtime, memory, parameter counts, or behavior as channel count grows. This is important because the proposed unified attention can be expensive for high-dimensional sensor systems.

The spectral distortion analysis is overstated relative to the evidence. The frequency-domain comparison in Table 6 shows extremely small differences between CTF and TimeXer, yet the paper uses this to support broad claims about interpolation-free modeling.

Presentation quality is below the expected bar in places: tables are dense and hard to read, some extracted values appear malformed, and the prose contains repetition and occasional grammatical/formatting issues.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored practical forecasting setting: multivariate series with channel-specific sampling periods and block-wise test-time missing intervals.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer has a coherent architecture: channel tokens provide a natural bottleneck for variable-length channel representations, while masked attention separates local temporal modeling from cross-channel exchange.

Evaluation is fairly broad for time-series forecasting, covering modified public benchmarks, a real industrial LNG dataset, conventional forecasting benchmarks, multiple strong baselines, error bars over seeds, ablations, and robustness studies.
The ablations support the main design choices: channel dependence, dynamic patching, and patch masking each contribute, with patch masking especially important under block missingness.
The paper is clearly motivated and generally well written, with useful analysis of interpolation-induced spectral distortion and frequency-domain behavior.
weaknesses: The main practical benchmarks are largely constructed by manually downsampling standard datasets; the realism of the chosen sampling periods and missingness processes is plausible but not strongly validated against deployment data.

Baseline fairness is a concern: most baselines are forced into interpolation or zero-filling pipelines, while the proposed model is designed for masks and variable channel lengths. Stronger comparisons to irregular/missing time-series models adapted for forecasting would make the evidence more compelling.

The novelty is solid but not transformative: channel/global tokens, masked attention, patch masking, and frequency-based patching are sensible combinations of known ideas rather than a clearly fundamental algorithmic advance.

Block-wise missing experiments are concentrated mainly on SolarWind in the main text, with additional ETT results in the appendix; broader missingness evaluations across all datasets and missingness mechanisms would better support the robustness claims.

Reproducibility is only moderate: implementation details are present, but there is no clear statement about code/data release, and the CHS dataset appears proprietary or at least not obviously accessible.

Scalability remains a real limitation because unified attention over all local and channel tokens can become expensive for high-dimensional sensor systems; the paper acknowledges this but does not experimentally quantify the cost.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and realistic forecasting setting: multivariate time series with cross-channel dependencies, heterogeneous channel sampling rates, and block-wise missingness at test time.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer is technically coherent: channel tokens, mask-guided attention, frequency-aware patching, and patch-level removal of missing regions form a unified architecture that directly targets the stated setting.

The experimental section is broad, covering multiple adapted public datasets, two real-world datasets, many baseline families, ablations, scalability analysis, error bars, and additional conventional forecasting results.
The ablations support the usefulness of the main ingredients, especially dynamic patching and cross-channel token interaction, and the missingness experiments show consistent robustness trends.
The paper is generally clear and includes ethics and reproducibility statements, dataset descriptions, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The main evaluation setting is partly synthetic: several public benchmarks are manually resampled using heuristic channel-specific periods. This makes the practical scenario plausible but not fully convincing as evidence of real-world asynchronous forecasting performance.

The novelty is moderate. The method largely combines known ideas: channel tokens, masked attention, patch dropout/masking, and frequency-based patching. The paper's contribution is mainly integration for a specific setting rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is a concern. Regular baselines are forced through interpolation, while the proposed model is designed around the non-interpolated representation; irregular baselines are reimplemented or approximated, and ContiFormer is explicitly modified for efficiency, which may affect conclusions.

The missingness setup appears favorable to the proposed model, especially on SolarWind where missing blocks span exactly one patch length and the model is trained with random patch masking. It is less clear how robust the method is to arbitrary partial-patch missingness, misdetected missingness, or non-block missing patterns.

Performance gains are often modest, and some results show close or mixed comparisons, e.g. modified TimeXer is comparable or better on ETT2 in the appendix, and conventional benchmark results are not consistently state of the art.
The private CHS dataset cannot be released, limiting independent verification of one of the more compelling real-world claims.
The method may face scalability issues for high-dimensional multivariate settings due to quadratic token interactions; the paper acknowledges this, but the solution remains future work.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time because code is only promised upon publication, and several dataset construction choices and baseline adaptations would be hard to audit without released scripts.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: multivariate forecasting under heterogeneous channel sampling, cross-channel dependence, and test-time missing blocks.

The proposed architecture is coherent at a high level, combining channel tokens, mask-guided attention, frequency-based patching, and patch masking in a way that is plausibly suited to variable-length channel inputs.
The evaluation includes several public benchmarks, one private industrial dataset, multiple baseline families, ablations, error bars, and some scalability analysis.
The paper is generally readable and provides useful implementation details about dataset construction, patching, masking, and training settings.
weaknesses: The main contribution is not very novel. Much of the method appears to be a recombination of existing ideas: channel tokens from iTransformer/TimeXer-like designs, masked attention, patch dropout, FFT-guided patching, and interpolation-free handling of irregular/asynchronous inputs. The paper does not convincingly establish a strong conceptual advance beyond this combination.

The experimental setting is partly synthetic and may favor the proposed method. Several 'practical' datasets are constructed by manually downsampling standard regular benchmarks according to assumed channel-specific rates, then comparing against baselines that are forced through interpolation. This makes the central advantage partly a consequence of the constructed protocol rather than compelling evidence of broad real-world robustness.

Baseline treatment raises fairness concerns. Regular baselines are often given interpolated inputs, while CTF is designed to ignore forward-filled values and remove missing patches. Irregular/missing baselines are reimplemented or modified, and ContiFormer is approximated rather than faithfully run. These choices could materially affect conclusions, yet the paper provides limited validation that each baseline is optimized and competitive under the new protocol.

The reported gains are often modest. For example, in asynchronous forecasting, CTF is only slightly better than PatchTST/TimeMixer++/modified TimeXer on several datasets, and in some detailed tables it is not uniformly best across horizons or metrics. In the conventional setting, CTF is generally not state of the art, which weakens claims of a broadly superior framework.

The ablation evidence is not sufficiently convincing. Some components show very small effects, e.g. removing patch masking has nearly identical CMAE in Table 3 and only small degradation in several settings. Channel token count and channel embedding effects are also inconsistent. The analysis sometimes overinterprets small numerical differences.

The missingness evaluation is narrow and somewhat aligned with the method's mechanism. The main block-missing experiment is primarily on SolarWind with missing blocks set to exactly one patch length, which directly matches the patch-removal design. Additional missingness experiments are limited and use fewer baselines, with mixed results on EPA where CTF is not consistently best in CMSE.

The formulation assumes fixed channel-specific sampling periods and known valid masks, and future targets are assumed fully observed. This is a narrower and cleaner setting than many real irregular multivariate time series problems, but the paper's language repeatedly suggests broad real-world robustness.

The spectral-distortion argument is overemphasized relative to the empirical evidence. The frequency-domain differences in Table 6 are very small, and the theoretical discussion does not by itself show that interpolation is the dominant cause of baseline underperformance across datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code is promised only upon publication, the private CHS dataset cannot be released, and several baselines are reimplemented or approximated. This makes it hard to independently verify the stronger claims.

Overall, while the paper is understandable and has a plausible engineering direction, the novelty, fairness of evaluation, and strength of evidence are not sufficient for a top-tier AI conference acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed practical setting: multivariate forecasting with simultaneous cross-channel dependencies, channel-wise asynchronous sampling, and block-wise test-time missingness.
ChannelTokenFormer is a coherent architecture: channel tokens, mask-guided attention, variable patch counts, frequency-aware patching, and patch masking are well aligned with the stated problem.

The experimental section is broad, covering strong regular forecasting baselines, irregular-time-series baselines, missingness-aware baselines, several adapted public datasets, and one industrial dataset.
Results are consistently favorable in the proposed practical settings, and the paper includes useful ablations for channel dependence, dynamic patching, and patch masking.
The paper is generally clear and includes implementation details, dataset descriptions, error bars, scalability analysis, and an ethics/reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The main technical ingredients are mostly recombinations or adaptations of known ideas: channel/global tokens, masked attention, PatchDropout-style masking, and frequency-based patching. The novelty is more in the unification and setting than in a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Several key benchmarks are constructed by manually resampling originally regular datasets according to plausible domain assumptions. This is useful, but it weakens the claim that the evaluation fully reflects naturally occurring asynchronous real-world data.

The strongest missingness results are largely based on synthetic block masking, especially on SolarWind; the paper would be stronger with more naturally missing test-time data and broader missingness experiments across all datasets.

Baseline fairness is not fully settled. Many regular baselines are forced through linear interpolation, while some irregular baselines are reimplemented or approximated; in particular, the approximated ContiFormer may not reflect the original model’s best capability.
Performance gains are often modest on some datasets and metrics, and the paper does not provide statistical significance tests beyond error bars.
The private CHS dataset cannot be released, and code is only promised upon publication, limiting immediate reproducibility of part of the empirical evidence.
The method relies on known sampling periods, valid-observation masks, and fully observed forecast horizons; these assumptions may not hold in some real deployments.
Scalability remains a concern for very high-dimensional sensor systems because the attention mechanism still grows with token count, despite masking and token compression.
